'''''A History of Pi''''' (also titled '''''A History of {{pi}}''''') is a 1970 non-fiction book by [[Petr Beckmann]] that presents a layman's introduction to the concept of the [[mathematical constant]] [[pi]] ({{pi}}).<ref>{{Cite web|last=Drum|first=Kevin|date=December 2, 1996|url=http://members.cox.net/kdrum/Pi.htm|title=''A History of Pi'', by Petr Beckman|publisher=|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070704132350/http://members.cox.net/kdrum/Pi.htm|archivedate=July 4, 2007|accessdate=April 13, 2014}}</ref>

==Author==
Beckmann was a [[Czechs|Czech]] who fled the [[History of Czechoslovakia (1948–1989)|Communist government of Czechoslovak]] to go to the United States. His dislike of authority gives ''A History of Pi'' a style that belies its dry title. For example, his chapter on the era following the classical age of [[ancient Greece]] is titled "The Roman Pest";<ref>Thoreau, [http://highclearing.com/index.php/archives/2007/05/18/6435 Book Recommendation: A History of Pi] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716032203/http://highclearing.com/index.php/archives/2007/05/18/6435 |date=2011-07-16 }}</ref> he calls the Catholic [[Inquisition]] the act of "insane religious fanatic"; and he says that people who question public spending on scientific research are "intellectual cripples who drivel about 'too much technology' because technology has wounded them with the ultimate insult: 'They can't understand it any more.'"

Beckmann was a prolific scientific author who wrote several electrical engineering textbooks and non-technical works, founded Golem Press, which published most of his books, and published his own monthly newsletter, ''Access to Energy''. In his self-published book ''Einstein Plus Two'' and in Internet [[Flaming (Internet)|flame wars]], he claimed that the theory of relativity is incorrect.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Farrell |first=John |date=2000-07-06 |title=Did Einstein cheat? |url=https://www.salon.com/2000/07/06/einstein/ |access-date=2022-03-25 |website=Salon |language=en}}</ref>

==Bibliography==
''A History of Pi'' was originally published as ''A History of {{pi}}'' in 1970 by Golem Press. This edition did not cover any [[Approximations of π|approximations of]] {{Pi}} calculated after 1946. A second edition, printed in 1971, added material on the calculation of {{Pi}} by electronic computers, but still contained historical and mathematical errors, such as an incorrect proof that there exist infinitely many [[prime number]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gould |first=Henry W. |author-link=Henry W. Gould |date=1974 |title=Review of A History of π |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2005843 |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=28 |issue=125 |pages=325–327 |doi=10.2307/2005843 |jstor=2005843 |issn=0025-5718|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A third edition was published as ''A History of Pi'' in 1976 by [[St. Martin's Press]]. It was published as ''A History of Pi'' by Hippocrene Books in 1990.<ref>"[http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/125074.A_History_of_PI A History of PI by Petr Beckmann] ", ''GoodReads''</ref> The title is given as ''A History of Pi'' by both Amazon<ref>{{ASIN|0312381859|A History of Pi}}</ref> and by WorldCat.<ref>{{OCLC|472118858}}</ref>
